category_title: Students who engage in disruptive behavior to escape or avoid writing tasks
minimal_context: Benjamin is sitting at his desk during independent work time with the goal of writing sentences.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time for independent work. Please get out your paper and start writing your sentences.

STUDENT: Did you know that some superheroes can fly faster than an airplane? Whoosh!

TUTOR: Please focus on your assignment.

STUDENT: (Shuffles his red, yellow, and green cards around on the desk) I'm making a traffic light with these cards. Red means stop!

TUTOR: You need to leave the cards alone and start writing your sentences now.

STUDENT: I can't, I'm too busy! The green card means go, so the cars are driving super fast! Vroom! I'm not doing this writing stuff!

options.A: Provide Benjamin with access to similar, but more socially appropriate, sensory stimulation by giving him a squishy stress-relief ball.
options.B: Conduct scaffolding conversations in chunks over the course of the independent work time, coming and going before resuming the next part.
options.C: Proactively contact Benjamin's parents, using a translator if needed, to share both successes and concerns regarding his independent work.
options.D: Implement escape extinction where Benjamin and the writing task remain in the classroom during independent work time.
